unit.title: Determine and plan for electrical installation requirements

summary: This unit teaches you to find out what a client's electrical installation needs before anything is designed or priced: the client's brief, the site survey, the load assessment and maximum demand, the choice of supply, special locations, Jamaica's climate, standby and solar power, approvals and outside bodies, and an outline programme and estimate. You will learn to write the requirements up as a schedule the client signs, and to handle changes to it.

blocks.p: Every installation starts with a question: **what does this building actually need?** A hotel kitchen, a clinic with vaccine fridges and a seaside bar do not need the same things. If the requirements are wrong, the design will be wrong, the price will be wrong and the client will be unhappy. This unit is for Level 3 trainees who will lead the planning of small and medium installations: homes, shops, offices, clinics, small hotels and workshops.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Meet the client (and architect), use a checklist, and find out how each area will be used, what equipment is planned and what growth is expected.
Record the existing supply, board, earthing, wiring and routes; measure the rooms; note the environment and anything unsafe.
List every load with its rating and pattern of use, find the connected load, apply the demand factors given and find the maximum demand and line current.
Decide between 110 V-only, 110/220 V split-phase and three-phase, and agree it with JPS early.
Plan for special locations and the environment
Pools, bathrooms, kitchens, outdoor areas, salt air, heat, hurricanes, lightning and flooding.
Pick the essential loads, plan a changeover switch and the generator size; check a roof for PV.
JPS, the government electrical inspection, the local authority and others, in the right order and early.
Prepare the programme, resources and estimate
Stages, long-lead items, calibrated instruments, a take-off and a cost estimate with contingency and GCT.
Write up and agree the requirements
A room-by-room schedule of points and a summary the client signs; handle later changes as variations.
Give trainees suitable survey tasks and check their work.

flow: Client brief
Drawings and site survey
Load list and maximum demand
Supply choice, agreed with JPS
Special locations, environment, standby and solar
Approvals, programme, resources and estimate
Written requirements, signed by the client
Design and pricing can begin

blocks.note: Requirements come **before** design. You do not choose cable sizes or breakers here; you find out what the installation must do, so the designer (next unit) can do that correctly.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The **brief** is the client's written statement of what they want the installation to do. Clients rarely write a good one on their own, so you take it from them with a checklist and write it up.

head: Topic
Questions
rows: What happens in each room now, and later? A 'storeroom' may become an office; a 'spare room' may become a hair salon.
A/C units, water heaters, stove, pumps, kitchen equipment, machines, lifts, computers, servers, security and data systems. Ask for the makers' data sheets.
When do the big loads run? A bakery's ovens at 4 a.m. and a restaurant's kitchen at 7 p.m. matter for maximum demand.
What must keep running in a power cut: fridges, a server, security lights, a water pump, medical equipment?
Does the client want to lower bills with PV, LED lighting, sensors or timers?
Another floor, more units, a second shop? Plan spare capacity now.
What the client can spend, when they must open, and any stage dates.
Does an owner's brand, an insurer or a franchise set extra requirements, such as emergency lighting or a fire alarm?

ul: Floor plans with room names and uses, furniture layouts and ceiling plans, from the architect.
Sections and elevations where ceiling heights and wall types matter.
The site plan: where the JPS pole, the service entry and any generator or PV can go.
For an existing building: old drawings, test records, the circuit chart and a year of power bills.

blocks.h: When the client asks for something unsafe

blocks.p: A client may ask for an ordinary outlet beside the shower, lights in the pool, or no earthing 'to save money'. Explain the risk plainly, say what the code and the specification allow, and offer a safe place or a safe method. You are paid for your judgement, not only for wiring what you are told.

blocks.note: Write the brief up and send it back to the client to confirm. 'What you told me' in writing is the start of the signed requirements, and it stops 'but I asked for…' arguments later.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **site survey** is the visit made to record the existing conditions before the requirements are written. For a new building it checks the site and the supply; for an extension it also checks everything already installed.

ul: Ask for drawings, test records, the circuit chart and recent bills.
Prepare survey sheets, a floor plan to mark up, a laser distance meter and tape, a torch, a camera and a clipboard.
Agree with the owner when you can visit without stopping their trade.

head: Item
Record
rows: Single-phase 110/220 V or three-phase; the service cable; the meter; the main switch rating and its condition; where the JPS pole and service drop are.
Make, age, number of ways and **spare ways**, main breaker rating, overheating or rust marks, labelling and the circuit chart.
The earth rod and its connection, the main earthing conductor, bonding to water pipes and metalwork.
Type, age, condition; damaged or overheated cable; poor work; rodent damage.
Measurements of each room; the existing lights, outlets, switches and data points, marked on the floor plan.
Where new cables can run; walls, beams, ceilings, ducts and other services in the way.
Salt air, damp, heat in the roof space, flood marks, lightning history, wind exposure.
Trips and faults, when work can be done, what they plan next.
Exposed live parts, missing covers, burnt outlets: report at once, in writing.

blocks.note: A survey is **visual**. Do not remove covers or open live boards on a survey. Where a board must be opened, it is done by an authorised person with the circuits isolated and the right PPE. Trainees look, measure and record; they do not open equipment.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Give trainees tasks that match their level: measuring rooms, recording existing points, taking photos, listing nameplate data. Decisions about the size of the service, the price and signing the requirements stay with the Level 3 planner and the firm.
The **load assessment** turns the client's list of equipment into the figures that size the supply, the main switch, the main cable and the board.

head: Term
Meaning
How it is found
rows: The total of the ratings of every load installed, before diversity.
Add every item's rating (W or kW) from its nameplate or data sheet.
The share of the connected load expected to run at the same time.
Given in the design data, the specification or the code the Centre uses, by type of building and load.
The largest load the building is expected to draw at one time. It sizes the supply.
Connected load × demand factor, plus an allowance for future loads.

blocks.p: Diversity is applied because **not all loads run at full power at the same time**: the stove, the water heater and all the A/C units are seldom at full load together. Without diversity the service would be oversized and expensive. With too much diversity it would be overloaded.
For each item record: what it is, its rating, how many there are, its voltage (110 V or 220 V), and when and how long it is used. A list of furniture or of staff numbers does not size anything.

blocks.h: Worked example: a house in Spanish Town

blocks.p: The design data gives a demand factor of 0.65 for this type of house: maximum demand = 22.45 × 0.65 = **14.6 kW**. The client plans a fourth A/C unit later, so allow 1.5 kW more: about **16.1 kW** to plan for.

On a 110/220 V split-phase supply, with the load shared evenly between the two lines, the current in each line is **maximum demand ÷ 220 V**: 16 100 ÷ 220 = about **73 A**. So a 100 A service, main switch and main cable would be planned, and checked with JPS. If the load were all at 110 V on one line, the same power would draw twice the current: that is why big loads go on 220 V and why the 110 V circuits are shared between the lines.

head: Sum
Method
Example
rows: Total current ÷ limit per circuit, rounded **up**
2 640 W at 110 V = 24 A; at 10 A per circuit = 2.4, so 3 circuits
Circuits needed × (1 + spare fraction), rounded up
1.8 kW × 6 h × 30 days = 324 kWh a month

blocks.note: Use the demand factors your instructor or the specification gives, and show your working. An examiner, and later an inspector or JPS, wants to see where every figure came from. Work each sum twice.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: For a compressor, a pump or a lift motor, find its supply voltage, its **full-load current** and its **starting current** (often several times full-load for a moment). Starting current matters for the volt drop other users will see, for the breaker type and for sizing any generator.

When adding to an existing building, compare the new total with what is there. An existing 100 A service with a measured maximum demand of 70 A and 40 A of new load gives 110 A: over the rating, so an upgrade of the service, main switch, cable and board must be planned with JPS. Never fit bigger breakers to an old board to make new loads 'fit', and never run large new loads from existing outlet circuits or extension leads.

JPS supplies most of Jamaica at 50 Hz, as single-phase **110/220 V split-phase** or as **three-phase**. The load assessment, the kinds of load and what JPS can give at the site decide which the building needs.

head: Supply
Conductors
Suits
Why
rows: A very small home or shop with lights, outlets and small appliances
Large loads draw high currents at 110 V, so cables, the service and the volt drop become unreasonable. Not suitable for stoves, water heaters or large A/C units.
Two lines and a neutral; 110 V from each line to neutral, 220 V between the lines
Most Jamaican homes, small shops, offices and clinics
Lights and outlets at 110 V; A/C, stove, heater, pump at 220 V, drawing **half the current** of the same power at 110 V.
Factories, hotels, plazas, large offices, buildings with large motors or lifts
Carries large loads with smaller cables; three-phase motors (pumps, compressors, lifts) start and run smoothly.

blocks.h: Why 220 V for the big loads

blocks.p: Power = voltage × current. A 2.2 kW pump at 110 V draws 20 A; at 220 V it draws 10 A. Half the current means a smaller cable and **a much lower volt drop** on a long run, such as a pump 60 m from the house. A 30 kW restaurant kitchen at 110 V would draw about 270 A: the cables, service and main switch would be huge. Hence split-phase or three-phase for anything above a small home.

Tell JPS the expected maximum demand and the kind of supply wanted as soon as you know them. JPS decides what it can supply, where the service and meter will go, and whether its line or transformer needs upgrading, which can take weeks or months. A large or three-phase supply, or a grid-tied PV system, needs JPS's own approval and paperwork.

blocks.h: Placing the main switch and board

ul: Near the supply entry, where it can be reached quickly and safely in an emergency: not in a locked bedroom, a roof space or behind cupboards.
Above any likely flood level in low-lying areas.
In a dry, ventilated place with working space in front of it.
Where the main cable routes can be agreed with the architect and the other trades at the planning stage, to avoid clashes with ducts, pipes and beams.

blocks.p: Some places need more protection than an ordinary room, and Jamaica's climate attacks equipment in ways a planner must allow for. List these **as requirements**, so the design and the price include them.

head: Location
Why it is special
Requirements to list
rows: Wet skin and bare feet lower body resistance.
No ordinary outlet within reach of the bath or shower; GFCI (RCD) protection; switches outside or out of reach; equipment rated for damp.
GFCI protection for outlets near sinks; dedicated circuits for stove, water heater and heavy equipment; enough outlets so adaptors are not needed.
Wet bodies, bare skin and metal all around the water.
Listed on their own; GFCI protection; bonding of metalwork; lights and equipment of the types the code allows; distances from the water kept.
Outdoor areas: beach bars, car parks, patios
Weatherproof outlets and fittings with GFCI protection; sun-resistant cable or conduit; nothing set in the sand or lying on the ground.
Each computer leaks a little current to earth; together they can trip an RCD.
Enough separate circuits that normal leakage does not trip the protection; surge protection; earthed outlets everywhere.
Places of assembly: cinemas, churches, halls, hotels
Many people must escape in a fire or blackout.
Emergency escape lighting and exit signs; fire alarm as the authorities and the insurer require.
Equipment must not lose power or be damaged by surges.
Dedicated circuits, surge protection, UPS where even a short break is not acceptable, standby supply.
Fuel stations, LPG stores, paint shops
Equipment certified for the hazardous zone, as the specification says.

head: Condition
Effect
Requirement
rows: Corrodes enclosures, glands, fixings and terminals; rusts boxes within a year or two.
Corrosion-resistant enclosures (stainless steel, GRP or coated), stainless fixings, and a suitable **IP rating** (the two-figure code for protection against dust and water).
A cable in a hot roof space carries less current; A/C loads are large; equipment in the sun runs hot.
State where cables will run so they can be **derated**; allow for cooling loads; shade or ventilate equipment.
Outdoor A/C units, PV frames, service masts and signs can be torn off.
Fixings rated for high wind, to the maker's and the specification's figures; a standby supply where loss of power matters.
Surges destroy TVs, computers and controls.
**Surge protective devices (SPDs)** at the main board and near sensitive equipment, with good earthing and bonding.
Boards, outlets and motors under water must usually be replaced.
Main board, meter, outlets and equipment placed above the likely flood level.
A low earth resistance is hard to get.
Ask about ground conditions early; allow for more or deeper rods or another electrode type.

blocks.note: Write the environment into the requirements, not into a conversation. 'Outdoor lights at the beach bar: corrosion-resistant, IP-rated for wet locations, GFCI protected' is a requirement a designer can price. 'Use good stuff near the sea' is not.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Power cuts happen, so many clients want some loads to keep running. Do not simply 'put everything on the generator': that makes the set large and costly. Plan it in steps.

flow: List the **essential loads** with the client: vaccine fridges, some lights, the server, security, a pump, perhaps one A/C
Find each one's rating and starting current
Work out the essential maximum demand with the diversity given, and add a margin for motor starting and growth
Group the essential circuits on their own **essential board**
Feed that board through a **changeover (transfer) switch**, manual or automatic, interlocked so the generator can never feed back into JPS's lines
Ask how long the client must run in a long outage, to size the fuel tank
Decide whether loads that cannot stand even a short break, such as a server, need a **UPS** as well
Plan where the generator stands: ventilation, exhaust, noise, fuel safety and access

blocks.note: A generator connected without a proper changeover switch can back-feed JPS's lines and kill a line worker, and will be destroyed when the JPS supply returns. The changeover switch is a requirement, never an option.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Before promising a client a roof-mounted PV array, check the **roof**: its strength for the panels and their frames, the direction it faces, shading from trees and buildings, and the space available. In Jamaica fixed panels generally face **south**, tilted at a low angle, to collect the most sun over the year. Check where the inverter and any batteries can go, and whether the client wants to export power: a grid-tied system needs JPS's approval and its own paperwork before it can connect.

ul: LED lighting with daylight and occupancy sensors cuts a large share of a building's lighting cost.
Timers and sensors on outdoor and corridor lights.
Efficient A/C units sized for the room, with the building shaded and sealed.
Water heaters on timers, or solar water heating.
Put these in the requirements if the client wants lower bills.

head: Body
What they decide
When to contact
rows: The supply it can give, the service and meter position, any line or transformer upgrade, approval for grid-tied PV.
As soon as the maximum demand is known: lead times can be long.
Licensed electrical inspector, under the Government Electrical Regulator (GER)
Inspects and certifies the installation before JPS connects it.
Find out the requirements at planning; allow time for the visit and any corrections in the programme.
Where the building, the service, the meter and the generator can go.
With the architect, before positions are fixed.
Insurer, fire service, brand or franchise
Fire alarm, emergency lighting, special standards.

blocks.p: Building these in early avoids two kinds of trouble: delays at the end while waiting for an approval, and rework when an approval asks for changes to finished work.

Break the job into stages: containment and first fix; boards and sub-mains; second fix; testing; inspection; JPS connection; handover. Fit them into the builder's programme. Mark the **long-lead items** (main switchboard, generator, transfer switch, special fittings) and order them early: a board ordered late holds up the whole job.

ul: People: electricians and helpers for each stage, with competent people for boards and testing.
Plant and tools: access equipment, cable-pulling gear, benders.
**Test instruments, with their calibration dates**, so calibrated instruments are on site when tests are due.
Materials: delivered when needed and stored safely.

flow: Start from the agreed requirements, drawings and schedule of points
Do a **take-off**: count outlets, lights, switches, boards and equipment; measure cable and containment runs; add an allowance for waste (often about 10%)
Price materials from current supplier quotes
Estimate labour hours per stage from past jobs, times the hourly rates
Add plant hire, testing and commissioning, inspection and JPS fees, transport
Add overheads and profit
Add a **contingency** for unknowns
Add GCT at the current rate
State what is included, what is excluded, the assumptions, and how long the prices hold

head: Sum
Example
rows: 18 circuits with 25% spare: 18 × 1.25 = 22.5, so a 24-way board

sections.title: Writing up, agreeing and changing the requirements

blocks.p: Write the requirements up as a **room-by-room schedule of points**: for each room, the lights, switches, outlets, data points, A/C supply, special equipment, and any special protection. Add a **summary** of the supply, the maximum demand, the standby and PV plans, the special locations, the environmental requirements, the approvals needed, the outline programme and the estimate.

head: Room
Points
Notes
rows: 4 × 110 V outlets, 2 × LED panels, 1 switch, 1 data point, 1 × 220 V A/C supply with isolator
Outlets at desk height on the examination side
2 × 110 V outlets for vaccine fridges on the **essential** board, 1 × LED panel, 1 data point
Fridge outlets labelled; alarm on the fridges
1 × LED fitting, switch outside the door
4 × pole lights on a photocell, 1 weatherproof GFCI outlet

ul: Both sides mean the same thing: the scope for the design and the price is agreed.
The designer and the team have a clear target.
The estimate is fair and complete, and anything later is clearly extra.
A signed record settles arguments about what was promised.

blocks.p: When the client adds a commercial kitchen halfway through planning, or three more A/C units, the change touches everything: the load assessment, the supply and the board, the special locations, the cost and the programme. Write the request down, confirm it, work through its effects, send a written **variation** with the extra cost and time, and wait for written approval. Then update the schedule, the drawings and the programme so everyone works from one version.

blocks.note: The items that are NOT part of determining requirements: choosing breaker brands, the colour of cover plates, the team's lunch breaks. Keep the requirements about what the installation must do and where.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can take a client's brief with a checklist and write it up for confirmation.
I can explain what to do when a client asks for something unsafe.
I can carry out a visual site survey and record the supply, board, earthing, wiring, rooms, routes and environment.
I can lead trainees on a survey and give them suitable tasks.
I can list loads with ratings and patterns of use, find the connected load, apply demand factors and find the maximum demand.
I can turn a maximum demand into a line current on a split-phase supply and choose a service size.
I can explain why diversity is applied and why big loads go on 220 V.
I can compare 110 V-only, split-phase and three-phase supplies and say which suits which building.
I can explain why JPS is contacted early.
I can list the requirements for bathrooms, kitchens, pools, outdoor areas, offices with computers and places of assembly.
I can set requirements for salt air, heat, hurricanes, lightning, flooding and rocky ground.
I can plan a standby supply with essential loads, a changeover switch and a generator size.
I can check a roof for PV and say what JPS needs for a grid-tied system.
I can list the approvals and outside bodies and when to contact each.
I can prepare an outline programme with long-lead items and a resource list.
I can do a take-off and build a cost estimate with contingency and GCT.
I can write a room-by-room schedule of points and explain why the client signs it.
I can handle a change to the requirements as a variation.

terms: Brief
The client's statement of what they want the installation to do.
Changeover (transfer) switch
A switch that connects a board to either JPS or the generator, never both, so the generator cannot back-feed the lines.
Connected load
The total of the ratings of every load installed, before diversity.
Contingency
A sum in the estimate for unknown costs.
Demand (diversity) factor
The share of the connected load expected to run at the same time.
Derating
Lowering a cable's current rating because of heat, grouping or insulation.
Essential load
A load that must keep running in a power cut, such as a vaccine fridge or a fire pump.
IP rating
The two-figure code showing how well an enclosure keeps out dust and water.
Long-lead item
An item that takes a long time to deliver and must be ordered early.
Maximum demand
The largest load a building is expected to draw at one time; it sizes the supply.
Schedule of points
A room-by-room list of the outlets, lights, switches and other points the client needs.
Site survey
The visit made to record existing conditions before the requirements are written.
Spare capacity (spare ways)
Capacity left on a board or service for loads added later.
Specification
The document that sets the required standard of materials, workmanship and testing.
Split-phase supply
Two lines and a neutral: 110 V line to neutral, 220 V between lines.
Surge protective device (SPD)
A device that limits voltage spikes, for example from lightning.
Take-off
The list of materials and quantities counted and measured from the drawings.
Three-phase supply
A supply with three line conductors, for large buildings and large motors.
UPS
Uninterruptible power supply: a battery unit that keeps equipment running through a short break.
Variation
A written change to the agreed requirements with its cost and time, approved before work.

c1.title: A bakery and café in Linstead
c1.text: Mrs Campbell is converting a shop in Linstead, St Catherine, into a bakery with a small café. Her list of equipment includes two 6 kW ovens, a 3 kW proofer, a 2.2 kW mixer, three display fridges, four 1.5 kW A/C units, a 3 kW water heater, lighting and outlets. The connected load adds up to 38 kW. The design data gives a demand factor of 0.6 for this kind of premises. The existing shop has a 110/220 V split-phase service with a 60 A main switch and a full 12-way board. She hopes to open in four months.

c2.title: A villa on the cliffs at West End, Negril
c2.text: Shane, a Level 3 trainee, is surveying the site for a new four-bedroom villa on the cliffs at West End, Negril, 40 m from the sea. The owner wants a pool with underwater lights, an outdoor kitchen and bar, a 220 V pump for the water tank 50 m from the house, and a standby generator for the fridges, the pool pump, security lights and the Wi-Fi. He also asks for an outlet 'right by the shower' in the master bathroom, and mentions adding two guest cottages 'in a few years'. The ground is limestone rock.

c3.title: A dental clinic in Ocho Rios
c3.text: A dentist is fitting out a two-room clinic on the first floor of a plaza in Ocho Rios. The plan has two surgeries with dental chairs and compressors, an X-ray room, a sterilising room with an autoclave, a reception with four computers, and a small server cabinet. The dentist has lost equipment to lightning surges at a previous clinic in the hills above Ocho Rios. The plaza's landlord can offer a three-phase supply or a 100 A split-phase supply to the unit. The dentist wants the surgeries to keep working through short power cuts.

c4.title: Estimating a community centre in Hayes
c4.text: Marlon is preparing the requirements and an outline estimate for a new community centre in Hayes, Clarendon: a hall for 150 people, two offices, a kitchen, toilets and a car park. The take-off shows 260 m of 2.5 mm² cable before waste. The hall is 20 m by 12 m, and the design data gives a lighting allowance of 8 W per square metre. The hall's lighting runs at 110 V and no lighting circuit may carry more than 12 A. The parish council (municipal corporation) must approve the building, and JPS has said a new transformer may be needed on the road.

c5.title: A school expansion in Brown's Town
c5.text: A private school in Brown's Town, St Ann, is adding a computer lab with 30 computers and a science room to an existing block. The existing 100 A split-phase service had a logged maximum demand of 64 A over the last term. The new rooms will add about 30 A. The school asks whether the main board, which has four spare ways, will do. The principal signed the schedule of requirements last week, and now asks for a 220 V kiln in the art room as well.

questions.q: With a connected load of 38 kW and a demand factor of 0.6, what maximum demand should Mrs Campbell's bakery be planned for?
questions.why: Maximum demand = connected load × demand factor = 38 × 0.6 = 22.8 kW. Dividing by the factor (63.3 kW) is a common mistake; the full 38 kW would ignore diversity.

questions.q: If the 22.8 kW is shared evenly between the two lines of a split-phase supply, about what current flows in each line, and what does it mean for the existing 60 A main switch?
o: About 104 A: the service and main switch must be upgraded
About 52 A: the existing 60 A main switch will do
About 207 A: three-phase is the only option
About 38 A: the existing service has plenty of spare capacity
questions.why: Line current = 22 800 ÷ 220 = about 104 A, well above the 60 A main switch and above the 100 A size as well. The service, main switch, main cable and board must be upgraded, and JPS told early.

questions.q: The bakery has a four-month opening date. Which step should the planner take first after the load assessment?
o: Order the ovens so they arrive before the wiring starts on site
Contact JPS with the expected demand to learn the supply and lead time
Choose the brand of breakers to be fitted in the new main board
Book the government inspection for the week before the opening
questions.why: JPS decides the supply, the service position and whether its line or transformer needs upgrading, and that can take weeks or months. It is the longest lead time in the plan, so it is started first.

questions.q: Why does the planner list the bakery's kitchen separately in the requirements, instead of treating it like the café seating area?
o: Kitchen equipment is always supplied at 110 V to keep the area safe
The kitchen must have its own separate meter fitted by JPS
Water, sinks and heavy fixed appliances need dedicated and GFCI circuits
Kitchens are lit to a lower level than a café seating area is
questions.why: A commercial kitchen is a special location: ovens, the proofer and the water heater need dedicated circuits, outlets near sinks need GFCI protection, and the layout must be agreed with the kitchen fitter. Writing it separately makes sure the design and the price include this.

questions.q: The villa is 40 m from the sea. Which requirement should Shane write for the outdoor lights and outlets?
o: Standard indoor fittings, painted over to protect them from the salt
Corrosion-resistant, IP-rated wet-location fittings with GFCI protection
Bare copper earth wires run outside the walls to carry the salt away
Fittings mounted as low as possible so the sea breeze cannot reach them
questions.why: Salt air corrodes ordinary steel boxes and fixings in a year or two, and outdoor outlets are a shock risk. Specify corrosion-resistant materials, a suitable IP rating and GFCI protection, so the designer can select and price them.

questions.q: In the load list for the villa, the tank motor is entered as 2.2 kW on 220 V. What running current goes in the last column?
o: It draws half the current, so the volt drop on the long run is lower
A 220 V pump does not need an earth conductor on the supply cable
A 220 V motor always turns at a higher speed than a 110 V motor
JPS charges less for each kWh used by loads running at 220 V
questions.why: For the same power, doubling the voltage halves the current, and volt drop depends on current and length. The cable can be smaller and the pump will start and run properly at the end of a 50 m run.

questions.q: The owner asks for an outlet right beside the shower. What should Shane do?
o: Fit it as asked, since the owner is paying for the whole villa
Fit it at floor level so the shower water runs past and misses it
Explain the risk and offer a GFCI outlet placed out of the shower's reach
Refuse all outlets in the bathroom and leave it at that, with no offer
questions.why: Wet skin and bare feet make a bathroom a special location. A planner explains the risk and offers a safe alternative, rather than either wiring something dangerous or simply saying no.

questions.q: Shane's requirements for the standby generator list a changeover switch. What is its main purpose?
o: To let the generator and JPS share the villa's load together
To stop the generator feeding back into JPS's lines when the mains fails
To make the generator start faster on cool and damp mornings
To let the JPS meter run backwards while the generator is running
questions.why: A changeover switch connects the essential board to either JPS or the generator, never both. Without it, generator power can back-feed JPS's lines and kill a line worker, and the set is wrecked when the mains returns.

questions.q: The ground is limestone rock and the owner plans two cottages later. Which pair of requirements should Shane add now?
o: A second JPS meter, and a 110 V-only supply to keep things simple
Extra or deeper earth electrodes, and spare capacity for the cottages
A smaller main cable now, and an earth connection to the sea water
No earthing until the cottages are built, and a board that is full
questions.why: Rocky ground makes a low earth resistance hard to get, so plan for it early. Known future loads call for spare ways and a service and main cable sized for them now, which is far cheaper than an upgrade later.

questions.q: The dentist can have a three-phase supply or a 100 A split-phase supply. Which fact decides the choice?
o: Three-phase is always cheaper to install than a split-phase supply
The maximum demand and the kinds of load, such as compressors
The number of patients the clinic expects to treat each day
The colour of the cover plates that the dentist has chosen
questions.why: The supply is chosen from the load assessment: the maximum demand, the current it gives on each option, and whether any equipment needs three-phase. The planner then confirms what the landlord and JPS can give.

questions.q: The dentist has lost equipment to lightning before. Which requirement answers that?
o: A larger main breaker so that it can carry the surge current
Longer cable runs so that the cables soak up the surge energy
Surge protective devices, with sound earthing and bonding
Changing the clinic to a 110 V-only supply to lower the voltage
questions.why: Lightning surges are limited by SPDs with short, straight earth connections, backed by sound earthing and bonding. Breaker size and cable length do nothing against a surge.

questions.q: The surgeries must keep working through short power cuts, and the reception computers must not lose data. Which plan fits the brief?
o: Put the whole plaza on one generator with no changeover switch
An essential board with a changeover switch, and a UPS for the server
Extension leads run from the neighbouring shop during each cut
Tell the dentist to close the clinic whenever the power fails
questions.why: Essential loads go on their own board fed through a changeover switch to the generator. Loads that cannot stand even the few seconds before a generator takes over, such as the server, need a UPS as well.

questions.q: The reception has four computers and the server cabinet. What should the requirements say about their outlet circuits?
o: Plain two-pin outlets so the computers are not earthed at all
Enough circuits that normal leakage does not trip, plus surge protection
One outlet circuit for the whole clinic to keep the board small and simple
Outlets taken from the X-ray room circuit, since both are electronic
questions.why: Each computer leaks a small current to earth; many on one RCD-protected circuit add up and trip it. Split them across circuits, keep them earthed, and add surge protection and dedicated circuits for the server.

questions.q: The take-off shows 260 m of 2.5 mm² cable. Allowing 10% for waste and terminations, how much should Marlon order?
questions.why: 260 × 1.10 = 286 m. The allowance covers offcuts, drops at each box and the lengths used at terminations.

questions.q: What lighting load should Marlon plan for the 20 m by 12 m hall at 8 W per square metre?
questions.why: Area = 20 × 12 = 240 m²; 240 × 8 = 1 920 W. The allowance is a planning figure; the designer will confirm the fittings with a lighting calculation.

questions.q: The hall lighting runs at 110 V and no lighting circuit may carry more than 12 A. What is the least number of lighting circuits for the hall?
questions.why: 1 920 W ÷ 110 V = 17.5 A. At 12 A per circuit, 17.5 ÷ 12 = 1.45, which rounds up to 2 circuits. A planner always rounds up.

questions.q: Why should the community centre's requirements list emergency escape lighting, when the offices next door have none?
o: It is a place of assembly: people must find the exits in a fire or blackout
Halls use more electricity, so every light needs a battery backup
The municipal corporation requires it for every car park it approves
Escape lighting takes the place of fire extinguishers in a hall
questions.why: Buildings where many people gather need emergency lighting and exit signs so they can escape when the normal lighting fails. The requirement comes from the authorities, the insurer and good practice, and must be in the plan and the price.

questions.q: JPS says a new transformer may be needed, and the municipal corporation must approve the building. How should Marlon show this in the plan?
o: Leave both out, since they are not electrical work for the planner
Contact both early; put their lead times and the inspection in the programme
Ask the client to deal with both of them after the wiring is finished
Book JPS for the opening day and hope the new transformer is not needed
questions.why: Outside bodies set lead times the planner does not control. A transformer upgrade can take months, and the building approval affects where the service and meter can go, so both go on the programme at the start.

questions.q: With a logged demand of 64 A and 30 A of new load, what should the planner conclude about the school's 100 A service?
o: 94 A is under 100 A, so it can take it, with little spare left
The new load must all go on one line to balance the board
The service must be upgraded, since the breakers will trip
The service is fine because the old demand was under 70 A
questions.why: 64 + 30 = 94 A, which is under the 100 A rating, so the service can carry it, but only about 6 A is left. The planner should warn the school that any further growth, such as the kiln, will need an upgrade, and check the board's ways and condition.

questions.q: A week after signing the requirements, the principal asks for a 220 V kiln in the art room. What should the planner do?
o: Add it to an existing outlet circuit, since the schedule is already signed
Tell the school a kiln can only be added after the handover is complete
Check the effects on load, board and cost, then issue a written variation
Fit it without charge to keep the client happy and the school onside
questions.why: A kiln is a large 220 V load. It may push the 94 A demand over the 100 A service and needs its own circuit and board way. The change is recorded, its effects checked, priced as a variation and approved in writing before the documents are updated.
